body: In paragraph 1, “clouded in anonymity” most nearly means that Jibhi was:

options.text: crowded with visitors from across the world
not widely known to potential visitors
closed to visitors by an official prohibition
already transformed into a concrete town

explanation: The phrase is used in contrast with Srinagar’s many tourists. In this context, anonymity means being little known. The later growth and concrete buildings appear in paragraph 3, while no official prohibition is stated.

sources.text:
[1] I was posted in Srinagar in the 1980s. Its mountains, rivers and meadows reminded me of my native Jibhi Valley in Himachal Pradesh. Srinagar welcomed many tourists, while Jibhi remained clouded in anonymity. I left the Indian Army and returned home to start tourism there.
[2] My family eventually agreed to let me turn our traditional house into a guesthouse. I kept its original character and added windows for sunlight. When I put up a signboard in 1992, villagers doubted that the venture would succeed. The business grew, but tourism took years to develop in the valley.
[3] A government homestay scheme in 2008 accelerated growth. People built homestays, villages became towns and concrete buildings multiplied. Local businesses and tourists put increasing pressure on nature. During the 2020–21 pandemic, tourism stopped. Residents returned to farming, pottery and government work schemes. They hoped tourism would return, but the pause also offered a chance to reflect and seek sustainable solutions.
[4] Tourism introduced me to people from many countries and Indian states. I learnt about different cultures, and many visitors returned as clients and friends. I feel proud that I fulfilled my dream and helped establish tourism in my home valley, yet humbled by what the journey taught me.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: Applying the passage’s tourist-welcome description to Jibhi would support A, but the word “while” assigns that description to Srinagar and contrasts Jibhi with it.
Anonymity might be mistaken for deliberate concealment from visitors, but the phrase does not say Jibhi was officially prohibited from receiving them.
Projecting the later growth of towns and concrete buildings back to paragraph 1 might suggest D, but the passage places that development later.

reasons: Paragraph 1 contrasts Srinagar welcoming many tourists with Jibhi remaining “clouded in anonymity”; in context, Jibhi was not widely known to potential visitors, so B is supported.

A transfers Srinagar’s tourist welcome to Jibhi, contrary to the contrast. C adds an official prohibition not expressed by the phrase. D conflicts with the passage’s later account of villages becoming towns and concrete buildings multiplying.
No authenticated comparator was supplied. This original practice question needs no past-paper counterpart.

body: An automobile company divides work into production, purchase, marketing, accounts and personnel. Which of the following is a disadvantage of this organisation structure?

options.text: It may lead to an increase in cost.
Managers may gain power, assert independence and ignore organisational interests.
It ensures that different functions get due attention.
Heads do not get training for top management positions.

explanation: Dividing work into production, purchase, marketing, accounts and personnel departments forms a functional structure. NCERT lists among its disadvantages that functional heads do not get training for top management positions because they cannot gather experience in diverse areas. Ensuring that different functions get due attention is an advantage of this structure.

sources.text: departments creates a functional structure. All departments report to a coordinating head. For example, in a manufacturing concern division of work into key functions will include production, purchase, marketing, accounts and personnel. These departments may be further divided into sections. Thus, a functional structure is an organisational design that groups similar or related jobs together.

(f) It ensures that different functions get due attention. Disadvantages: The functional structur e has certain disadvantages which an organisation must take into consideration before it adopts it. Some of them are as follows: (a) A functional structure places less emphasis on overall enterprise objectives than the objectives pursued by a functional head. Such practices may lead to functional empires wherein the importance of a particular function may be overemphasised. Pursuing departmental interests at the cost of organisational interests can also hinder the interaction between two or more departments. (b) It may lead to problems in coordination as information has to be exchanged across functionally differentiated departments. (c) A conflict of interests may arise when the interests of two or more departments are not compatible. For example, the sales department insisting on a customer friendly design may cause difficulties in production. Such dissension can prove to be harmful in terms of fulfillment of organisational interest. Inter ­ departmental conflicts can also arise in the absence of clear separation of responsibility. (d) It may lead to inflexibility as people with same skills and knowledge base may develop a narrow perspective and thus
have difficulty in appreciating by other point of view. Functional heads do not get training for top management positions because they are unable to gather experience in diverse areas.

The divisional structure has certain disadvantages. Some of them are as follows: (a) Conflict may arise among different divisions with reference to allocation of funds and further a particular division may seek to maximise its pr ofits at the cost of other divisions. (b) It may lead to increase in costs since there may be a duplication of activities across products. Providing each division with separate set of similar functions increases expenditure. (c) It provides managers with the authority to supervise all activities related to a particular div ision. In course of time, such a manager
may gain power and in a bid to assert his independence may ignore organisational interests.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: A cost increase is a recognised disadvantage when divisional structures duplicate activities; the supplied excerpt does not identify it as a functional-structure disadvantage.
Managers gaining power and ignoring organisational interests is attributed to divisional structure in the excerpt, not to the functional structure identified here.
The excerpt confirms this as a functional-structure feature, but it is an advantage, whereas the question asks for a disadvantage.

reasons: The listed departments group related functions, identifying a functional structure (E1.1).
The excerpt states that functional heads do not get training for top management positions because they lack experience across diverse areas (E3.1); this supports D.
C describes a functional-structure advantage (E2.1), not a disadvantage. The cost increase and manager-power options are described for divisional structure in the supplied excerpts (E4.1, E5.1).

body: A museum marketing manager divides event work into graphic design, registration enquiries and bill payments, but gives each team member responsibility for an entire event rather than allocating these tasks. She holds regular feedback meetings, yet task quality suffers. Next season she allocates the tasks according to each member’s skills and competencies. Which organising step was previously not performed properly and is now performed?
explanation: The earlier tasks were identified, but allocation to staff did not follow their skills. The change explicitly matches tasks to competencies, which is assignment of duties. A: Task categories were already identified in the earlier season. B: The described correction is allocation by skills, not a reporting-line change. C: No creation or regrouping of departments is described. D: The source expressly matches allocation of jobs to employee skills and competencies.

sources.text: Assignment of duties: It is necessary to define the work of different job positions and accordingly allocate work to various employees. Once departments have been formed, each of them is placed under the charge of an individual. Jobs are then allocated to the members of each department in accordance to their skills and competencies. It is essential for effective performance that a proper match is made between the nature of a job and the ability of an individual. The work must be assigned to those who are best fitted to perform it well.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: Whole-event responsibility might seem to mean work was not divided among people; however, the stem explicitly divides the work into three task types.
Feedback meetings could suggest reporting links, but they were already held before the change; the new action described is skill-based task allocation.
The listed work categories might be mistaken for departments, but no new departmental grouping is described; the changed action is assigning tasks by skill.

reasons: The stem says event work was divided into named tasks, so identifying and dividing the work is already described.

The change is to allocate tasks to employees according to their skills and competencies. E1.1 defines assignment of duties as allocating work to employees in accordance with their skills and competencies, so D fits.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: The manager divided work initially, so she was engaging in division of work.
Regular feedback meetings establish communication channels, representing reporting relationships.
Grouping event activities constitutes departmentalisation.

reasons: Under NCERT Business Studies (Organising process), 'Assignment of duties' entails allocating specific jobs to members in accordance with their skills and competencies, ensuring a match between job nature and individual ability.

The stem states that the manager had already divided the event work into components, but initially gave each person an entire event rather than allocating specific tasks; she subsequently allocates tasks according to each member's skills and competencies, which exactly corresponds to 'Assignment of duties'.

body: In a hypothetical budget policy, the government supplies free food grains to households with low incomes. Which budgetary objective is most directly illustrated?
explanation: Transfers targeted to low-income households change disposable income and its distribution. That is the redistribution objective directly illustrated; other possible macroeconomic effects are not the objective specified. A: The case focuses on who receives a transfer, rather than production-resource allocation. B: No cyclical stabilisation target is stated. C: The low-income transfer directly illustrates redistribution. D: Instability is not the stated objective.

sources.text: The government sector affects the personal disposable income of households by making transfers and collecting taxes. It is through this that the government can change the distribution of income and bring about a distribution that is considered ‘fair’ by society. This is the redistribution function

option_challenges.strongest_reading: The policy shifts food resources to households, but the stated low-income targeting most directly indicates a change in income distribution, not a general resource-allocation objective.
Food aid might affect demand or hardship, but the stem gives no stabilization context; the targeted transfer directly signals redistribution.
The policy could be destabilising only with an unstated disruptive effect or aim; neither is indicated by the targeted provision described.

reasons: Free food grains targeted to low-income households are a benefit that changes their access to resources. The excerpt states that government transfers can change household disposable income and distribution—the redistribution function (E1.1).

The low-income targeting makes redistribution the most direct objective. A generic shift of resources does not make reallocation the more direct objective; the stem supplies no stabilization context, and it does not illustrate economic instability.
This is an original-practice item with no authenticated comparator supplied; no past-paper counterpart is required.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: The policy diverts public resources towards producing or procuring food grains for social welfare rather than commercial goods.
Supplying food stabilizes consumption against price fluctuations and macroeconomic volatility.
The policy causes fiscal deficit leading to macroeconomic instability.

reasons: According to NCERT Macroeconomics, the redistribution function of the government budget focuses on altering the distribution of income to achieve a fairer distribution in society, accomplished through taxes and transfers (in-kind or cash) to households.

Providing free food grains specifically to low-income households is an in-kind transfer intended to support their real consumption and reduce income disparity, which directly illustrates the 'Redistribution of income' objective.
